item.title: Dinner Is the New Meditation
item.description:
Attention

Dinner Is the New Meditation

A three-star chef, a Zen master, and the quiet art of attention while cooking.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Our minds wander almost half our waking hours, and research shows a wandering mind is an unhappy one.
  • Cooking holds our attention through smell, sound, and touch. Making a meal can lift our mood the next day.
  • The care we put into a meal reaches the people we feed, but only when we’re truly present.
Source: BonzEarthsnapper/Adobe Stock

Many of us treat cooking as a form of work, where the goal is to get to the food, and the process is just one more form of labor that we have to get through if we want to enjoy the reward at the end.

And when we work, our minds wander. We rehearse tomorrow’s meeting while we chop the onions. We keep our phone on the counter and check messages while keeping an eye on the pot. Dinner gets made, but we are barely there in the making of it. Our bodies are in the kitchen, but our minds are far away, pre-occupied with issues that seem more important.

But cooking can be much more than this. For me, it is how I slow down, how I focus my attention, and how I care for the people I love. Eric Ripert, the chef behind New York's three-Michelin-starred Le Bernardin, draws the reader into this kind of cooking in his new book, Mindful Cooking: Simple Recipes for Nurturing Body and Soul. Ripert’s goal in the book is to encourage cooks to approach their task with more attention and less anxiety, an approach that grew out of time he spent in Buddhist monasteries in Japan and Korea. Ripert applies these techniques in his restaurant. As he told AARP, "A cook who's shaking will not cook better than a cook who's precise." But this is not just a lesson for the pros. The mindset Ripert cultivates carries over to the home cook as well, and, more importantly, to life in general.

The trouble with being somewhere else

A 2010 study published in Science found that human minds frequently wander. In fact, the group sampled reported that their minds were on matters other than the task at hand nearly 50% of the time. And the more someone’s mind wandered, the lower their happiness, regardless of the activity they were engaged in.

There are many techniques that can help pull us back into the moment we are inhabiting. But for me, cooking is the most intuitive. It is a regular part of the day for most people, and its technical demands can force us to focus if we choose to do more than simply heat some ingredients up.

The fragrant waft of garlic in butter or oil is one of the most beguiling scents you will encounter in the kitchen. But the garlic can turn bitter in seconds if left over too high a heat. A sauce can break while we are distracted. A steak can turn from pink to gray in minutes while an egg yolk can become rubbery and unappetizing. Unless we pay attention to the pots and pans in front of us, a delicious meal can turn into something uninspiring … or worse.

But if we retain our focus and refuse to let our minds drift away, the rewards go beyond a pleasant plate of food. The act of cooking becomes an act of creation. And that in itself yields important benefits. Psychologist Tamlin Conner and her colleagues found that creative activities, including cooking, are associated with greater positive emotion and flourishing. That doesn’t mean we should treat cooking as a cure-all for the stresses of modern life. But the creativity and focus involved in intentionally making something with our hands is a powerful counterbalance to a day of screens and deadlines.

What Japan taught me

My understanding of cooking took on a new depth during a series of journeys I took through rural Japan with my late friend and mentor, Ito San. Alongside many other things, Ito San introduced me to kaiseki, the Japanese tradition of carefully composed, seasonal dining. In the course of these travels, I also came to appreciate shojin ryori, the vegetarian cooking of Zen Buddhist temples, where nothing is rushed and nothing is wasted. In both of these traditions, cooking is much more than a chore. Instead, it is elevated almost to the level of practice for living well.

This approach to cooking has deep roots in Japan. In his Instructions for the Cook, written in 1237, the Zen teacher Dōgen recounts coming across an elderly monk drying mushrooms under the hot sun. Dōgen asks why he does not leave the task to a younger person. The monk’s reply has stayed with me since I first heard the story. He says to Dōgen, “Someone else cannot do my work for me.”

Dōgen shares the same thought in a different way elsewhere in his book. "When you boil rice,” he writes, “know that the water is your own life." Life is, in many ways, the sum of the small tasks we complete. None are without meaning if we choose to make them our own.

Steadying the hand

On Sunday afternoons, I will normally leave my phone in another room while I prepare dinner. Slowly, the week falls away, and all that is left is the cutting board in front of me.

The meal might be a procession of complex dishes. Or it might be something as simple as masoor dal, the red lentils my mother used to make. In either case, the meaning is mine to find. My mother is no longer here, but the movements she taught me have survived; they are reflected in my hands. Her love is in the way I cook, and the act of cooking is itself an act of remembrance.

The same practice has helped me stay devoted to my son, who is a cancer survivor. Illness teaches you how little you control. In the kitchen, I can still do something with my hands that channels my full attention toward someone I love. Ripert is right that a cook who is shaking does not cook well. Neither does a parent. Cooking steadies me, and my son needs me steady.

An invitation, not an obligation

Cooking should not become another self-improvement assignment, another standard to judge ourselves harshly against. Not everyone has the time or energy or inclination to cook from scratch every night, and a task that restores one person may be a burden to another. The point is rather to take note of the opportunities we have for paying attention, and to use them instead of seeking distraction.

If you cook tonight, leave your phone in another room. Notice the onions as they soften. Taste before adding more salt. When you sit down to eat, give the people at the table the same attention you gave the food.

We spend so much of our lives trying to get to the next thing. But sometimes, the next thing can wait.

item.title: ADHD and Sensory Overload in Parenting
item.description:
ADHD

ADHD and Sensory Overload in Parenting

Why everyday noise can trigger distress for adults with ADHD.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Adults with ADHD can experience intense sensory distress, especially from everyday parenting noise.
  • Parenthood limits sensory management strategies that adults with ADHD used before having children.
  • Sharing sensory challenges with family and planning responses can ease parental distress.
Source: Pexels/JiriDockal

“A baby's cry to me was so overwhelming ... it was like sensory pain.”

This is a quote from my colleague and ADHD coach, Clay Gill, during our conversation about the ins and outs of parenting with an ADHD brain. Clay explained that, before becoming a father, he had wondered whether he wanted children because he found the sound of babies crying so overwhelming. After his daughter was born, he experienced intense physical distress when she cried.

Clay described the feeling vividly: being unable to think clearly, experiencing an intenseurge to escape, and sometimes freezing or becoming very agitated.

We often think of sensory sensitivity as being associated with autism alone, yet a growing body of research suggests that many people with ADHD also experience heightened sensitivities to their environment, particularly in relation to auditory and visual processing.

As Clay articulately described, many adults with ADHD can modify their environments to accommodate for sensory sensitivity prior to having children: using noise cancelling headphones to avoid the grating sound of someone’s chewing, staying away from physical touch if it makes you irritable, staying indoors during bright sun. However, once children arrive on the scene, parents cannot always implement many of these sensory-saving habits. You must change the dirty diaper even as the baby squeals, follow your child’s story while being distracted by the too loud TV, or accompany your shy child to a chaotic birthday party in a event room with bright fluorescent lights.

Source: Pexels/PavelDanilyuk

For parents with ADHD, sensory overload may be particularly challenging. The noise, movement, and constant interruptions of family life can also place demands on the cognitive processes that are often difficult for people with ADHD: regulating attention, filtering distractions, and managing emotional responses.

Source: Pexels/SilverkBlack

Some ADHD parents I see in my clinical practice tell me that their sensory sensitivities make it hard to respond to their children in the way they would like to. For example, you may find yourself unintentionally snapping at your child for something minor. This often leads many parents with ADHD to experience guilt and shame, especially if you know your child did not do anything wrong.

So, what is a sensitive ADHD parent to do? Start with noticing when you feel this way: what are the sensory sensitivities that really challenge your ability to cope during family time? Which ones are a 10/10 stressful, and which ones are easier to handle?

Make a list and share it with a trusted support person, perhaps a co-parent. Create and share a plan for when you may need to leave a parenting situation, and which ones you can try to handle. For older children, explain your sensory sensitivities to them and ask their ideas on how you can all help manage better when the situation arises. Also, think about what helps you after your sensory sensitivities have been activated: a short walk, deep breathing, or some alone time.

Remember, being overwhelmed by the sensations of parenting does not mean you love your children any less. Nor does it mean you need to simply try harder to tolerate them. Understanding your sensory sensitivities and finding ways to work with your ADHD brain, rather than against it, can help you create a family environment that works better for everyone.

item.title: Why Being in the Here and Now Reduces Past Emotional Pain
item.description:
Mindfulness

Why Being in the Here and Now Reduces Past Emotional Pain

Mindful awareness shifts your awareness away painful memories and trauma.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Mindful presence shifts focus from painful memories to the safety of the current moment.
  • Practicing presence strengthens the brain's prefrontal cortex—boosting reflection and response.
  • Savoring simple, “in-between” moments helps encode joy and value into daily life.

Throughout my career as a psychotherapist, I’ve repeatedly heard the refrain “Who would I be without my (anxiety, depression, etc., fill in the blank)?” While clients express a need for change, they also have a deeply embedded fear of tearing down a well-crafted, life-long identity that is connected to their pain. This is more common than you might think.

For example, have you ever had memories of a trauma or past negative event replaying in your head like a favorite tune? We've all experienced this.

Fortunately, scientists have learned that present moment awareness shifts attention away from old triggers and past traumas. For example, a study conducted by the US. Department of Veteran Affairs concluded, "The relationship between lifetime trauma burden and various mental health issues of relevance to U.S. veterans may be mediated by mindfulness or the ability to pay attention to the present moment."

Getting into the here and now is good emotional medicine.
Source: Amadeo Valar/unsplash

So how do we get present and stop those unfriendly songs from playing over and over in our heads?

I know, that sounds like one of those “how do you change a lightbulb” jokes, but it’s worth considering, and may not be as daunting as it sounds.

Present Moment Awareness Rewires the Brain

The experience of being present in the here and now is now being applied in various ways in the therapy world. Mindfulness-Based Exposure Therapy, for example, is being used with combat vets, who are taught to move their awareness away from rumination and back to the present moment, where they can recognize that they’re safe and respond to what’s happening right around them.

Here's the kicker: Whether you know it or not, learning to get in the present moment strengthens the brain's prefrontal cortex, or what I call the Reflect and Relate Module of the brain.

When you practice presence, you strengthen the circuitry of the brain that helps you pause, think, and respond—rather than activate the react and get stressed system of the brain.

Three Easy-To-Use Practices for Getting Present

  1. Savor an In-Between Moment.

    Have you ever noticed how easy it is to lose sight of what’s happening right here, right now in your own “backyard”? The practice of noticing the in-between helps you to pause, come back to the moment, and steep yourself in the here and now.

    I’ll always remember the time when a client with acute depression shared with me a simple but profound in-between moment that had stayed with him that past week.

    He said to me, “I heard a bird chirp. That reminded me of springtime, and it gave me hope.”

    You can journal these “little, ordinary moments” to start. Make sure to share those moments with others. In this way, you are not only reflecting, but relating these little moments with others. By both reflecting and relating, the brain more strongly encodes these memories—and values them as precious moments that make up a life well lived!

  2. Find One Pleasant Thing in the Here and Now.

    The practice of noting pleasantness can help shift you out of negativity and toward joy. Let's try this right now by having you notice one pleasant thing in your surrounding environment. This can be a color (such as your favorite color), an object, a sound, or even a shape. You can continue this practice each time you step into a new room or space. As you do this, find yet one more pleasant thing.

    This repetition rewires the brain and trains you to get out of the head and into the here and now moment. If you do this enough times, it will become a fun habit for you to seek out pleasantness, whether you are on your computer, at home making a meal, or out shopping.

  3. Share Your “Strength” with Another.

    There’s a mountain of research showing how strength-based practices reduce depression and even enhance one’s own identity as a socially caring contributor.

    Let's try one of my favorite strengths practices right now. To do this, you'll start by naming your top three personal strengths. This could be anything, such as tenacity, enthusiasm, kindness, fairness, compassion, patience, encouraging, mentorship, discipline, perseverance, responsible, caring, thoughtful, sensitive, wise, intelligent, adaptable, understanding, and so on.

    Next, you'll choose one of those strengths and put it to use for the rest of the day. As you do this, how does makes you feel? You can journal all the times you put your strength to use. Remember that even if you apply your strength just one time a day, that's good enough! Continue using this strength for one entire week.

    The following week, you can put another of their key strengths into action—even just once a day for a week. Believe it or not, this was shown to be an effective way of enhancing mood and reducing depression.

    This is a wonderful way to get present and make a difference in your world as well.

Conclusion

As you practice the above-mentioned ideas, you'll not only be getting present, but you'll be rewiring your brain.

By practicing presence, you'll start to savor all the little and astounding things that are around you, whether you're driving your car or waiting in line at the store. Most importantly, you can use these presencing practices anytime that one of those old, unhappy songs starts playing in your head. Happy presencing!

item.title: What Children’s Play Can Tell Us About Their Language
item.description:
Child Development

What Children’s Play Can Tell Us About Their Language

Yvonne Johansen tackles the nuances of language sample analysis.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Language samples help identify children’s communication needs and guide therapy.
  • Time demands can keep speech-language pathologists from collecting language samples.
  • Engaging, child-led play can encourage children to talk and share stories.
  • Standardized tests may miss how a child communicates in everyday life.
Source: Kier in Sight Archives/Unsplash, used with permission

Understanding how a child communicates takes time. Sadly, a recent study suggests that time is a major obstacle for experts seeking to assess and assist children. In a survey of 337 U.S. speech-language pathologists (SLPs), only 60% reported using language sample analysis during the previous year, and 74% (of those who had not) identified limited time as a barrier (Wilder & Redmond, 2024).

This means many students are not getting properly assessed and—without a thorough understanding of students' challenges and needs—adults are hindered in their efforts to provide well-informed support.

Amid such challenges, how can we properly hear what children’s everyday communication reveals? To better understand the answer to that question and more, I chatted with Yvonne Johansen, a pediatric SLP trained at Teachers College, Columbia University, and the founder of SmartFelt Toys. Johansen's 35-year career has spanned Head Start programs, public schools, private practice, consulting for California's Regional Centers, and serving as Clinical Director of Pathways to Speech. I spoke with Johansen about the challenges of assessing children's language, as well as what adults can do to overcome such challenges and get students the support they need.

Jenny Rankin (JR): Language sample analysis (in which a child's language is recorded during play, conversation, or storytelling, then transcribed and analyzed) is considered the gold standard for assessing children's language. Why isn't it used more often?

Yvonne Johansen (YJ): As an undergraduate in the 1980s, I worked for the New York City Board of Education's Citywide Speech Services while attending classes. I distinctly remember my first language sample analysis. I immediately knew its importance, but transcribing a 50-utterance sample (about 50 things a child says) word for word and then analyzing it took hours and hours by hand.

When something is that time-consuming, avoiding it can become a temptation. So many SLPs let language sampling slip out of their diagnostic battery because it's simply not in the bandwidth of a school-based SLP.

There's software now for transcription and analysis, but getting the child to talk is still a challenge. In a 30-minute session, you need to build rapport and keep a child engaged long enough to get 50 or more utterances. You also have to change how you talk. This isn't a therapy session, and, let's face it, speech therapists talk a lot. To get a good sample, you have to become the copilot, not the pilot, and that's not easy for us to do.

JR: Why is a language sample necessary?

YJ: I've worked with many children who were able to answer questions on a standardized test but struggled to explain to me what had happened at school or why they were upset. A language sample allows us to hear how a child uses language to communicate. Research has found that certain aspects of how children tell stories and explain things at age 5 predict their reading comprehension at age 8 (Griffin et al., 2004).

The sample will also show us the child's content, form, and use of language. This helps determine eligibility for services. And beyond that, it gives us important information about what that child needs, and where their therapy should start.

JR:What have you discovered to overcome the obstacles to language sampling?

YJ: I worked with many children who wouldn't speak in the classroom, whispered, or spoke only to certain people. I learned that getting a child to talk isn't as simple as asking questions. You have to find something that engages their interest and draws them in.

With younger children, I've found that play is often the best place to start, assuming you can get the child interested. If they don't like what you're giving them to play with, they likely won't stick with it, and you won't get much language from them.

I've also learned not to ask too much, too soon from a child. Start with something they can easily manage, and build from there. Stay in their comfort zone.

Children enjoy toys they can handle and move around. A dollhouse or farm with people and animals gives them plenty to do and talk about. They can make up their own stories and decide what happens next. Children who are engaged talk more, providing you with language you might not hear if you're simply sitting across from them and asking questions.

JR:What should parents and teachers know, and what can they do at home or in the classroom?

YJ: Parents and teachers are usually the first to notice when a child has difficulty communicating, and their input matters. So it's imperative to pay attention to how a child talks about something that happened, explains an idea, or makes up their own story during play. And it's important to let them talk without asking a barrage of questions. Let them take the lead, while you follow it.

If you're concerned about the level of a child's language, share your observations and concerns with an SLP, and ask whether a language sample was part of their evaluation.

What matters most is getting a true real-life picture of how a child communicates, not just how they perform on a test.

item.title: We ‘Could’ See Everything
item.description:
Body Language

We ‘Could’ See Everything

Nathan Fielder’s documentary makes clear that relentless observation has limits.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • The film blurs lines between documentary, theater, and self-aware performance.
  • Body language often contradicts words, creating unease and ambiguity throughout the film.
  • Despite unprecedented access, the documentary questions if seeing truly equals understanding.
You Can See Everything
Source: Shutterstock / rblfmr

You Can See Everything, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is a revolutionary piece of filmmaking that blurs the boundaries between documentary, reality, and storytelling.

Elizabeth Holmes founded Theranos, a Silicon Valley company that promised to transform healthcare by performing hundreds of blood tests using just a few drops of blood. The technology failed to deliver on those promises, and Holmes was eventually convicted of defrauding investors and sentenced to more than 11 years in federal prison.

In 2023, shortly before reporting to prison, Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, invited filmmakers into their rented beachfront home in Del Mar, California. The documentary offers an intimate look into Holmes' life during those final weeks of freedom. We watch her prepare, both psychologically and practically, for her impending prison sentence, spend time with her two young children, navigate her relationship with Evans, and continue revisiting the technology and ambitions behind Theranos. Through zoomed-in conversations, ordinary domestic moments, and uncomfortable exchanges, we are given seemingly unprecedented access to one of Silicon Valley's most controversial figures.

When a Documentary Becomes Theater

You Can See Everything blurs the boundaries between documentary filmmaking, reality, and storytelling.

The cameras capture intimate family interactions, uncomfortable conversations, and ordinary domestic routines, but the deliberately composed shots and extraordinary close-ups give the film a theatrical quality.

Amanda Seyfried, who portrayed Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout, returns to play Holmes, this time with the intention of understanding the real woman, reenacting conversations and events that took place outside the documentary's scope.

The film becomes as much about the construction of a narrative as the narrative itself. We watch people going about their lives, but we also watch them respond to the knowledge that they are being observed, sometimes making it difficult to distinguish between spontaneous behavior and calculated performance.

No Straight Answers

Throughout the documentary, Fielder asks incessantly direct questions and makes blunt remarks, yet the answers seem to manage to go in circles.

In one exchange, he tries to help Holmes understand the difference between saying the Theranos machine can perform certain tests and saying it could perform them if the technology were developed.

It seems like a straightforward question and an easily understandable distinction, but the dialogue becomes increasingly confusing as Holmes continues defending her understanding of what she had promised as being congruent with what she claimed.

At one point, Fielder introduces the famous Abbott and Costello comedy routine "Who's on First?" to illustrate how language can create perplexity when people assign different meanings to the same words. It was mind-blowing how frequently this pattern repeated itself in the documentary.

Later, when Seyfried asks Holmes whether she knew Seyfried was visiting Evans, Holmes offers another evasive non-answer, where she says she doesn't know if she knew. Although this answer begs the interpretation that she, in fact, did know, it doesn't allow us to identify that as definite.

In my clinical work, this is an exchange that I witness regularly, when people deflect questions because they feel shame, fear, or emotional overwhelm. In some cases, the person is so invested in a narrative that considering another perspective feels threatening. And sometimes, of course, people deliberately avoid answering because they fear the consequences.

Decoding Facial Expressions

Holmes frequently appears with unusually wide eyes, raised eyebrows, and repetitive nodding, especially in moments when she is challenged about her actions or asked to acknowledge responsibility. At times, her words communicate reassurance and certainty while her facial expressions appear confused, even frightened.

Interestingly, during more ordinary interactions, such as announcing that she is going outside or taking a phone call, her demeanor appears congruent with her statements, and her incessant nodding and surprised expression subside.

Fielder's body language and facial expressions in response to Holmes is very readable, His jaw often drops, and his brows frequently lift in disbelief when Holmes offers an evasive answer or seems unable to understand the point he is trying to make.

Evans' facial expressions are also fascinating to watch. At times, his reactions appear immature, almost childlike, while at other moments he seems visibly stressed or intimidated by the direction of a conversation. Occasionally, he appears so uncomfortable that he leaves the conversation altogether.

In psychotherapy, we pay close attention to moments when someone's body language or facial expression seems incongruent with the story they are telling.

When someone describes a painful childhood experience while smiling or making a dismissive comment about the event, as a therapist, I might gently nudge the client toward curiosity about the discrepancy. Perhaps they have learned to minimize their emotional needs, or defending their parent has become a way of preserving an important relationship, or embracing the sadness feels too overwhelming.

We learn to understand the world through other people's body language and facial cues. Children search their caregivers' faces for reassurance, danger, affection, and trustworthiness. When something unfamiliar happens, a caregiver's frightened expression may increase the child's distress, while a calm, reassuring demeanor can help the child feel safer.

When someone's body language and gestures seem inconsistent with their words, we may experience discomfort because the signals are difficult to reconcile.

Holmes' sustained eye contact, wide eyes, constant nodding, and sometimes seemingly-fixed expressions create ambiguity and uneasiness and raise questions about the words she is saying. The film repeatedly invites us to confront this incongruence.

Some of the documentary's most emotionally intense moments for me were Holmes' grief around the approaching separation from her children. To me, her sadness and tears about being apart from her young kids felt extremely genuine and painful.

We Could See Everything, But Did We See Anything?

Despite the access, intimate conversations, emotional revelations, and almost relentless close-ups, the documentary leaves a lot of questions unanswered.

Fielder and Oppenheim have created an artistically profound work by challenging the assumption that seeing more necessarily means knowing more.

Being able to relate to another person requires curiosity, context, and a willingness to question our own interpretations. It's important to remember that we are listening to someone's story, and our interpretation of it is inevitably influenced by our own experiences, emotional state, and level of vulnerability in the moment.

The camera can show us someone's face, but it cannot give us direct access to their internal experience or to the series of events that led the person to where they are.

I left this documentary thinking about how much we communicate without words, how carefully we construct the stories we tell about ourselves, and how readily we believe we can make sense of another person simply by watching them.

item.title: Small Steps, Lasting Impact
item.description:
Education

Small Steps, Lasting Impact

The impact of those tiny modifications in making life changes.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Starting with tiny, manageable changes is easier and leads to lasting habits.
  • Nearly half of our daily actions are habitual, often done on autopilot.
  • A recent study found that combining small changes in three areas was linked with lifespan.
  • Consistent small improvements in sleep, activity, and diet may extend lifespan by a year.
That small step can be an important one in the change process.
Source: wal_172619/Pixabay

I complained to my friend that I was a slow cyclist. I had recently ridden in a 3000-person biking event where, it seemed, nearly everyone passed me at some point.

He surveyed my bike. “I think you need to raise your seat a little,” the friend said.

I followed his suggestion. The “little” tweak transformed my biking world.

I felt more extension in my legs. I was able to pedal with more efficiency and could even see things better from a slightly higher position.

The notion of “small changes lead to larger changes” was a gem that I learned years ago in my teaching. I still marvel at the meaningful simplicity of this idea.

Bill O’Hanlon focused on this specific premise in his 1999 book, Do One Thing Different. “Whenever you are stuck with a problem, try something new. Do something—just one thing—different. Break the pattern of the problem,” he wrote.

The idea still sticks with O’Hanlon. “It’s easier to make small changes than big ones,” he told me via email. “Easier to initially make them and then to make adjustments if they don’t work or if you want to make even bigger ones that follow the initial small change.”

Willpower and motivation aside in making behavior changes, the idea is to merely start small.

After all, our willpower is limited, a point to remember according to Ezekiel Emanuel in Eat your Ice Cream. “Do what you can, remembering that…small, habitual changes, especially ones you enjoy, make the longest-lasting impacts,” he wrote.

An estimated 43 percent of a day belongs to habits, often done when our minds are elsewhere, according to Wendy Wood. She cited research in her 2019 book that nearly 90 percent of daily hygiene, such as showering and dressing, was due to habits, and 55 percent of work-oriented tasks was done habitually.

If desiring a new habit, the key ingredient is reward. “All we have to do is repeat something and get rewarded for it, and we’re learning a habit,” she said in one interview.

The rewarding component is brain-related. When rewarded, the brain’s release of dopamine connects the context of the behavior and positive response. “That’s one of the reasons why rewards are so important and so useful for forming habits,” she said.

Small adjustments done concurrently may have surprising outcomes. Koemel et al. (2025) found that combining about five minutes of sleep, two minutes of moderate/vigorous exercise, and the equivalent of a half-serving of vegetables or whole grains to daily routines was related to an additional year of lifespan.

The authors noted that “a potential synergy” may exist across the sleep, physical activity, and nutrition behaviors, suggesting that small modifications in them “may offer a powerful and feasible public health opportunity for improving lifespan for at least a year...”

Those adjustments may just have a ripple effect, as O’Hanlon pointed out. “Changes in behavior can lead to changes in feelings, sensations, perceptions and physiology,” he said. “Everything is connected and each of our systems can affect one another.”

Making those seemingly minor positive changes in health might be surprisingly significant, at which point they may become second nature.

It’s akin to learning how to ride a bike: You’ll always know how to do it. Just remember to adjust the seat.

item.title: Pets Can Positively Influence a Child's Development
item.description:
Child Development

Pets Can Positively Influence a Child's Development

How caring for animals can support comfort, empathy, and responsibility.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Caring for pets teaches children empathy by respecting animal boundaries and needs.
  • Pet care routines foster responsibility but adults must ensure all pet needs are met.
  • Shared pet activities strengthen family bonds and provide meaningful shared experiences.
  • Choosing a pet should consider the whole family's needs, including the pet's temperament.

Imagine your child coming home after a challenging day at school. They failed a test. A so-called friend embarrassed them during lunch. You can tell they need space, so you don’t ask questions. You watch your child collapse onto the couch. The family dog immediately snuggles besides them. For a few minutes, there is nothing that must be done. There is just connection between two beings who love each other unconditionally.

Having a pet offers many benefits for children. A pet may offer companionship. It may teach a child about responsibility and respect and love. A pet may help a child manage anxiety, stress, or sadness. A pet in the home may lead to a child who develops a deeper sense of empathy and compassion.

Pets offer comfort during challenging life events

In a study of 101 children aged 7 to 12, researchers asked participants to complete stressful speaking and math problems. Children accompanied by their own dogs reported a smaller increase in stress than children accompanied by a parent or no support figure. The study did not find an overall difference between groups in the level of the stress hormone cortisol. [1]

That distinction is important. Feeling comforted is valuable, but it does not mean a pet completely eliminates anxiety. For some children, alone time with a family pet l may help make a difficult moment more manageable. If parents notice a child struggling, they can ask their child, “Would you like to have our pet sit by you?”.

It is important to respect your child’s response. Some kids would rather watch an animal from a distance, and some do not want animal contact at all. It is important to respect your child’s preference. At the same time, a family pet is not obligated to comfort anyone. A pet needs the freedom to move away; comforting a child is never an animal’s obligation.

Caring for a family pet deepens empathy

Empathy involves recognizing, understanding, and sharing the emotions of others. A child may want to cuddle a cat that wants to be left alone. That moment allows for the practice of self-control. A parent might say, “She’s walking toward her litter box. Let’s give her space.” This encourages observation and a behavioral response that is respectful and caring. Children can learn that demonstrating affection includes respecting boundaries.

An observational study surveying 1,646 parents found that preschoolers in dog-owning households were more likely to show prosocial behaviors and less likely to have peer problems. It is important to note that the study was observational. That means that the study cannot establish a causal relationship. Environmental circumstances may also contribute. [2]

Having a pet encourages responsibility

A dog’s water bowl needs refilling even when a child would rather ride their bike. Fish need to be fed even when a child has a homework assignment to complete. These tasks can provide practice an opportunity to follow through and contribute to family life. Consider starting with one manageable job, such as helping an adult fill a water bowl. Explain why it matters: “Fresh water keeps our dog healthy.” Specific information helps to connect the child’s involvement of care to the effect that their action has.

Adults need to remain responsible for making sure every need of the pet is met. If a child forgets to complete their pet-related chore, help them try again. An animal should never go hungry or without water in attempts to teach a lesson. As animals get older, children watch how adults respond when care is inconvenient. Calmly cleaning an accident or adjusting a routine for an aging pet provides an example of continued care and compassion. These moments provide families with an important lesson to discuss that caring continues even when it requires extra effort.

Shared pet-related routines can create connections

Walking a dog together as a family creates time for moving, being present, and engaging in meaningful conversation. Playing fetch with the family dog can encourage a loving bond while simultaneously keeping kids off of electronic devices.

The relationship may also provide a child with something meaningful to share: a funny story to tell their friends, a new picture to share with their grandparents, or the opportunity to help a pet learn a new skill or trick. Parents can follow the child’s interest and use it to engage in conversation. Yet it is important for a parent to set boundaries. Pets should never be expected to be a solution for friendship difficulties, loneliness, or mental health disorders.

Find a good match for your family

Before purchasing a pet, make sure that the arrangement works for everyone. Consider allergies, costs, time and energy available to care for the pet. It is also important to gauge the the child’s comfort level with the pet, as well as the animal’s temperament and needs. Please note, the majority of the research discussed in this blog relates to dogs; findings should not automatically be applied to every animal species.

A family pet can become a beloved companion. Additional benefits include providing an opportunity to practice kindness and compassion, as well as an opportunity to meet another’s needs and to show up consistently. Finally, family pets can lead to an experience of unconditional love. That’s a win for everyone.

item.title: 3 Ways Humanoid Robots May Change Our Children
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

3 Ways Humanoid Robots May Change Our Children

The psychological impact may be bigger than the technical one.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Children may bond and get attached to robots in complex ways that we do not anticipate.
  • Robots could help with your child's anxiety, or maybe fuel it.
  • Robots could change the dynamics of family relationships.

If you don't think robots will be making their way into our homes within the next three to five years, then you are likely in denial. As you read this, manufacturing facilities are being repurposed, and new industrial spaces are being built for the production of humanoid robots.

Just remember that smartphones were around before iPhones flooded our lives. By this I mean that humanoid robots may currently be where smartphones were before the iPhone, meaning they're already here. But we are still waiting for the big-splash moment (and it will be sooner rather than later) that makes millions of people want one.

"Invisible" Robots Are Already Among Us

It amazes me how little we talk about the impending mass influx of robots into our lives. Perhaps it is because we are more currently worried that AI will wipe out our current society before that happens. Seriously, though, just think about it: we are already getting used to living around robots.

For years now, shoppers in supermarkets have seen robots looking for spills on the floors and roaming about the aisles to also scan shelves. Just here in my neck of the woods, Pennsylvania, Giant supermarkets have Marty, a tall robot with googly eyes that has literally been rolling around their floors since 2019.

True confession time: I will sheepishly admit that one time when Marty was coming towards me, I attempted to have a stare-down with it (I lost, by the way). But guess what? Marty did not even know I was there, and the same goes for all the other shoppers that it "sees". Interestingly, based on my observations, most shoppers now barely look at him.

Why Robots In Your Home Is A Whole Other Story

Yet where things get really fascinating will be soon, when seeing the impact of robots when they are within your home. What happens when that robot has arms and legs, talks with your child, and remembers what they said yesterday? Pushing the envelope of true possibilities, what then happens when your robot notices your child is upset?

As a psychologist who has worked with children and families for decades, this gets very interesting to me. So much so that I will discuss below three ways that I think humanoid robots in your home may profoundly change your children's lives.

1. Children May Get Attached In Big Ways

I'm saying kids will get attached to robots because we know that children form attachments with all types of things. As parents, we find it amusing how stuffed animals get names, and they have personalities, feelings, and occupy an important place in our kids' lives.

Many years ago, I was desperately searching around a local park in the dark for Willy, one of my kid's beloved stuffed animals that was left there. Heck, the police officer who shone a light on me even felt compassion. Now, let's look from another angle if you think bonding with your family robot is ridiculous. How about the generations of Star Wars audiences who fell in love with R2-D2, that annoying as heck, beeping, rolling machine that looked more like a tin can than even a human (and R2-D2 was in a movie versus in your house)?

Research suggests that as robots look more humanlike, children may be more likely to attribute human qualities to them. That may seem like a pretty obvious assumption, by the way. But what if the robot bonding experience for your child goes beyond looks?

Let's say the robot remembers your kid's favorite song, watches your child practice a presentation and gives feedback, or senses your child had a rough day at school and asks your child about it? Can you see how a robot in your home is a whole different storyline than your toaster or dishwasher (though I was sad to get rid of a cherished burnt-out toaster recently)

2. Robots Could Help With Your Child's Anxiety, Or Maybe Fuel It

In my book, When Overthinking Overtakes Your Child, and in my direct work with anxious children, I encourage parents to help children learn to tolerate uncertainty instead of continually reassuring them. Now, imagine if you put a robot in your house and your kid asks, "Is Mom mad at me?" Or, maybe your anxious child asks, "Is Joey just pretending to be my friend"?

I'd like to think a thoughtfully designed robot would recognize that reassurance-seeking pattern and help the child use coping skills. But what if that robot is not very "psychologically-minded" and instead answers your kid's anxious questions every time? Or, what if your child is afraid of emptying the trash because of germ fears and asks that robot to take that on so the child no longer has to overcome their fear? What's my related fear, by the way? We could accidentally create the world's most available reassurance, enabling machines.

3. Robots Could Change The Dynamics of Family Relationships

I thought I'd save this most provocative point for last. But just suppose a child starts telling the family robot things that she does not want to tell her parents? Do you think that the parents are the ones that should be directly involved in those conversations?

While we're speculating, should the robot ever discipline the child? For example, let's say the parents are in another room and/or outside, and the robot sees the child do something not allowed. Now what? Or, what if the child is disrespectful to the non-human robot? It's a robot, after all, and not a human, but doesn't it still matter if the child is practicing being disrespectful or perhaps even cruel?

Closing Thoughts

Scientists and engineers have spent years trying to figure out how to make robots look and act more like us. The progress in humanoid robot advancements and the likelihood of them being part of our lives has been astounding, and their integration into our daily lives will occur sooner than we realize. Shouldn't we start thinking about how living with them will impact our children's lives?

item.title: Reclaiming Joy on All Hallows' Eve and Beyond
item.description:
Play

Reclaiming Joy on All Hallows' Eve and Beyond

Costumes give adults rare permission to play, but we can keep that spirit going.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Fun and play foster creativity and connection, yet adults often lose easy access to them.
  • Cultures around the world use costumes and masks to make fun more accessible.
  • Social media has made costume play a daily habit, with real benefits and real costs.
Eva at Museum Hotel with Dennis and Marquis
Source: Eva Ritvo

Real life is often funnier than fiction. Case in point. I wrote this post on Halloween in a witch costume, sitting in a museum hotel in St. Louis, where I'd come for a baby shower. It sounds like a game of Mad Libs, but every word is true.

After years of reflecting on kindness, I enjoyed the irony of my outfit. And I had plenty of company.

"Witch" is the most popular adult costume this year, according to the National Retail Federation's annual survey, with an estimated 4.8 million American adults planning to dress as one.

We Love to Pretend

We start doing it early. Children try on roles constantly: superhero, doctor, astronaut, princess, or monster. Pretend play is how kids test out identities and feelings. In a cape, a child can be brave for an afternoon and see how bravery feels. A toddler pushing a doll in a stroller is trying on what it might feel like to care for someone the way Mom or Dad does.

Adults rarely get that opportunity. Halloween gives it back to us. For one night, we can be spooky, silly, sexy, or whatever strikes our fancy.

And we take that fun seriously. The National Retail Federation expected half of Americans to dress in costume this year, spending about $4.4 billion. Even pets are part of this, with pumpkin and hot dog costumes topping their list.

Why Fun Matters

Fun can seem like a luxury, something we get to once the serious work is done. Psychologists suggest otherwise. Barbara Fredrickson's "broaden-and-build" theory proposes that positive emotions such as joy and amusement widen our attention and thinking in the moment. Over time, they help us build lasting resources such as creativity and resilience.

Fun also connects us. As the guest of honor at the baby shower put it, "Family is shared experience." Fun isn't a break from a good life. It is a large part of how we build one.

Tilly!
Source: Sandra Ritvo/with permission

Why Fun Comes So Easily for Kids

Watch children on Halloween, and you'll see genuine fun. They commit fully to being a dragon. They don't wonder whether the costume is flattering or what their friends will think.

Several things change as we grow up. In adolescence, self-consciousness rises sharply. Psychologist David Elkind described the "imaginary audience," the teenage sense that everyone is watching and judging. We learn to fear looking foolish, which is sometimes exactly what play requires, and it can take us a long time to outgrow that fear.

That is why Halloween gives adults such a rare pass. When everyone is in costume, the imaginary audience is too busy with its own outfits to judge ours, and for one night, we get to play like kids again.

Masks Around the World

Halloween isn't the only time people dress up to become someone else. In Brazil, Rio's samba schools spend much of the year making dazzling costumes so that, for one night, a seamstress or bus driver can dance down the avenue as royalty. In Mexico, Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) brings painted skull faces and La Catrina, the elegant skeleton who reminds us that underneath, we are the same.

Japan gave us the word cosplay, a blend of "costume" and "play." Today, fans worldwide spend months crafting costumes of anime, comic book, and video game characters. A mask can lower the stakes of being seen. Freed from our usual role, we can express more sides of ourselves and find joy in the process.

Every Day Is Halloween Online

For many of us, though, the most constant dress-up party now happens on our phones.

On Instagram and TikTok, we can try on a new look any day of the year, and a filter adds glitter, cat ears, or flawless skin with a tap.

Much of this is genuinely good. Like children playing pretend, people can experiment with style and identity at little cost. Creators who rarely saw themselves in magazines, including people with disabilities, larger bodies, and older faces, now share images on their own terms.

But a Halloween costume and a filter are different. On November 1, the costume goes back in the closet, and nobody expects us to show up to work as a vampire. A filter can quietly become the face we think we should have.

Artificial intelligence has raised the stakes. With a few taps, AI can smooth skin, reshape a face or body, or place us in outfits and places we've never been. Some popular "influencers" don't exist at all. We may find ourselves comparing our ordinary faces to people who were never real.

Play also changes when it is scored. On Halloween, the reward is the fun itself. Online, likes can turn play into habit-forming performance. In a UCLA brain-imaging study, teenagers' reward circuitry responded more strongly to photos that appeared to have many likes. A Halloween costume delivers its joy and then comes off. The pull of likes never quite ends.

Taking Off the Mask, Kindly

Joy and Vince as Aqua and Terra getting married and living happily ever after.
Source: Eva Ritvo

The lesson of Halloween: Maybe the best costumes are temporary. They let us try on courage, glamour, or mischief, then return to ourselves with a little more of it.

And Halloween is only the first party of this season. From Diwali to Thanksgiving, Hanukkah, Christmas, Kwanzaa, and New Year's, the coming weeks offer more chances to gather, celebrate, and play, when the darkest days might otherwise pull us inward.

On the morning after, it is worth asking a few questions. What did my costume let me be? Can I bring some of that into an ordinary day? And when I look at a photograph of myself without a costume or a filter, can I look with the same delight?

As for me, the witch costume is back in the closet until next year. The Joy, I'm keeping. (Pun intended.)

item.title: How Major Life Events Brought About My Schizophrenia
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

How Major Life Events Brought About My Schizophrenia

Positive stress can also spur psychosis and schizophrenia.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • I have never experienced any significant trauma but still developed schizophrenia.
  • Some people are destined to develop schizophrenia and others may or may not depending on life events.
  • The positive stress of entering college perhaps led to my first psychiatric symptoms.
  • Marijuana use, even one time, can lead to an ongoing psychosis where antipsychotic medication is needed.
Source: Scronfinixio / Pixabay

When I present my story of full recovery from schizophrenia, I am often asked the question, “What trauma brought on your schizophrenia?”

The answer is simple: I have never experienced any significant trauma or neglect. Of course, everyone has bad days. But there was never any significant abuse, bullying, or painful breakups with a significant other.

People with and without schizophrenia make up a spectrum. Most people will not develop schizophrenia, even if they endure severe hardship. On the other hand, people like me have schizophrenia encoded in their DNA (or at least this is what my doctors believe). No matter what happens to us in life, we are going to develop the illness. This group is part of the 1 percent of people worldwide who develop schizophrenia.

Then there are individuals in the middle of the spectrum. These people may or may not develop psychosis, depending on their life experience, as well as their developmental experience during gestation. Unborn babies with a mom who has diabetes or other health conditions will be at a much higher risk of developing schizophrenia later in life. If there is any difficulty or trauma as a child, they will be at higher risk as well. Smoking cigarettes can also lead to a higher risk.

And finally, for many individuals, drugs like marijuana have the potential to set off a psychotic episode that may never subside without antipsychotic medications, and treatment may be indicated for life. Sometimes a psychosis will begin following just a single use of marijuana.

New school and research

Looking back, though there was an absence of trauma in my life, there were stressful life events.

The first one I recall is leaving my home in the suburbs of Cleveland, Ohio, to attend the University of Southern California. Going to USC was my dream. Packing to go, then finally arriving and moving into the honors dorm was the most exciting thing I had experienced to that point in my life.

As soon as I arrived, I wanted to find a molecular biology research laboratory to work in. I found one within days of arriving in Los Angeles. I remember spending time in the lab doing experiments often until the early hours of the morning. I loved the lab, but it was incredibly stressful.

Travel

When I began my junior year at USC, I was searching for something more in life. Unfortunately, I didn't use my restlessness to further my chosen educational goals; I looked for more through international travel and planned a two-month trip to Nairobi.

I loved Africa and had a wonderful trip. But I felt a lot of stress.

I didn't know Swahili, beyond a few words (most spoke some English, but usually not very well). I greatly enjoyed helping some girls with their English, but that was stressful too. While living in the slum, we lived on vegetables. Later in the summer, I met a rich missionary and his wife, and they told me I looked pale and sick. I wasn't taking care of myself.

Travel was dangerous. People got around Nairobi on small buses called "matatoos," and though I occasionally traveled around the city, I rode in four separate matatoos that broke down. There was always the risk I would be attacked or hurt, as I was living right in the heart of a dangerous slum during my first few weeks. But I saw the breakdowns as a new adventure and dismissed the danger.

The culture was different and difficult to adjust to. It was very hard to find even two minutes to myself in the crowded house we lived in by the road. But I loved the sense of community and friendship.

I never imagined that on my return, this stress would cause a psychosis to take over my mind, and I would be unable to attend college again until 2009. I spent years homeless and symptomatic before making a full recovery from schizophrenia in 2008.

Looking back

Major life events, even positive ones like giving birth or traveling, can cause stress. This stress can bring on psychosis for a person who has a certain genetic composition (1,2,3,4).

Looking back, leaving to attend school in California was much more stressful than I had anticipated. Would I have done better academically and in my personal life if I had attended a university closer to home? I will never know the answer, but I do remember that USC was my ultimate high school dream. I did not finish my degree there, but I am grateful for the good experiences I had at USC. While I was in Africa, two research studies were published, one in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. I am still very proud of both of these papers today.

A person living with psychosis or another mental illness should be aware that stressful events, even if they are positive, can cause a return of psychiatric symptoms. I am grateful for my exceptional psychiatric care in Cincinnati that has kept me productive and happy for more than 18 years.
